title: Gad and Nathan's lost books are Samuel / Kings still extant
source_text: V. Jam vero quod attinet ad eos libros, quorum exemplo, adversarii probare contendunt, libros quosdam divinos & authenticos periisse, Dico, vel falsum esse quod perierint, vel eos nunquam Canonicos fuisse, & immediate a Deo inspiratos. Et quidem existimamus propheticos fuisse, & ad Canonem pertinere libros Gad Videntis, & Nathanis Prophetae, qui cap. ult. lib. 1. Paralip. junguntur libris Samuelis, & in quibus scripta fuisse dicuntur gesta regis David, tam prima quam novissima: sed negamus illos periisse, & etiamnum extare pertendimus. Sunt enim illi ipsi libri qui hodie libri Samuelis vocantur, sive, prout habet vulgata versio, primus & secundus Regum. Nam quod solus Samuel non sit illorum author, inde manifestum est, quod in medio libri primi mors Samuelis describitur. Non potuit ergo Samuel scribere ultra sexdecim circiter hujus libri capita. Reliquum vero libri, & alterum etiam librum, qui ex usu Judaeorum Samuelis etiam dicitur, quinam potius scripserint, quam Gad & Nathan Prophetae, qui tempore illo vixerunt, & illius historiae pars ipsi non minima fuerunt? Certe hoc satis aperte indicat ille ipse locus quem adversarii citant: Nam ibi Gad & Nathan Samueli junguntur, tanquam ejusdem Davidis historiae scriptores & continuatores.
pass_a_gloss: Now as to those books by whose example the adversaries contend that certain divine and authentic books have perished, I say either that it is false that they perished, or that they were never Canonical and immediately inspired by God. And indeed we judge prophetic, and belonging to the Canon, the books of Gad the Seer and Nathan the Prophet, which in the last chapter of 1 Chronicles are joined to the books of Samuel, and in which the deeds of king David, both first and last, are said to have been written: but we deny that they have perished, and we maintain that they still exist. For they are those very books which today are called the books of Samuel, or, as the Vulgate has it, the first and second of Kings. That Samuel alone is not their author is plain from the fact that in the middle of the first book Samuel's death is described. Samuel therefore could not write beyond about sixteen chapters of this book. As for the rest of the book, and also the other book which by Jewish usage is also called Samuel's, who rather wrote them than Gad and Nathan the Prophets, who lived in that time and were themselves no small part of that history? Certainly the very place the adversaries cite shows this plainly enough: for there Gad and Nathan are joined to Samuel as writers and continuators of the same history of David.
pass_b_english: For the cited lost books: either they did not perish, or they were never canonical immediate inspiration.
Gad and Nathan we count prophetic and canonical — but still extant as Samuel, Vulgate 1-2 Kings.
Samuel alone cannot be full author: his death falls mid-1 Samuel, so he stops around chapter 16.
The rest, and 2 Samuel, fit Gad and Nathan, who lived the story and are named beside Samuel as its writers and continuators.
